subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: I share a flat with Lokesh, so I saw this play out. Two weeks ago at the college canteen a senior kept mocking Pooja's stammer while about ten people laughed or looked away. Lokesh was there and said nothing; I know because Lokesh told me that night, sitting on the balcony staring at the street. Lokesh was quiet for days. Then on Friday Lokesh went and found Pooja and said, "I saw what happened and I did nothing. I am sorry." Pooja shrugged, said thanks, and then told Lokesh what it had felt like. I stood at the door. I think it cost Lokesh a lot to say it. Lokesh has already decided that next time it will be sitting beside Pooja straight away.

qa.q: What did the senior do at the college canteen?
qa.a: A senior kept mocking Pooja's stammer at the college canteen while about ten people laughed or looked away.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling during the days after the canteen?
qa.a: Lokesh felt regret and shame, staring at the street and staying quiet for days, which turned into a wish to apologise.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do with the shame instead of hiding it?
qa.a: Lokesh went to Pooja, admitted watching and doing nothing, apologised, and decided to sit beside Pooja next time.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Pooja to hear Lokesh's apology and then describe how it had felt?
qa.a: Pooja probably felt some relief at being seen and believed; shrugging and saying thanks before opening up suggests careful trust.

grounding: A young adult regrets watching and doing nothing, uses the shame to decide how to act next time and apologises to the person affected.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Monday. In the hostel lounge four people laughed as someone filmed Tushar tripping and spilling his tea, and no one helped. Ayesha stood at the doorway with her books, telling herself it was just a joke. Tushar left without a word. Tuesday. Ayesha could not concentrate. The picture of Tushar walking out kept replaying, and shame settled in her chest. Thursday. Ayesha knocked on Tushar's door. "I watched on Monday and did nothing, and I am sorry. If it happens again I will come over to you at once." Tushar looked surprised, then said, "Thanks for saying so." They sat and drank tea.

qa.q: What did Ayesha say when knocking on Tushar's door?
qa.a: Ayesha said, "I watched on Monday and did nothing, and I am sorry."

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling on Tuesday?
qa.a: Ayesha felt shame and guilt, unable to concentrate as the picture of Tushar walking out kept replaying.

qa.q: What turning point on Thursday moved Ayesha from shame to action?
qa.a: Ayesha knocked on Tushar's door, apologised for watching and promised to come over at once next time.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt when Ayesha knocked and apologised?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt surprised and a little comforted to learn that one person had noticed and cared; the thanks and the shared tea suggest relief.

grounding: A young adult regrets having watched and done nothing, and apologises to the person affected while deciding how to act next time.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Dear Amandeep, I am still shaking from this morning. Near the station a man collapsed on the pavement, and about thirty of us were walking past. I slowed down and looked at everyone else. Nobody stopped, so I thought maybe it is not serious, maybe he is drunk, maybe someone has already called. Then I saw his hand twitch and felt sick. I called out, "You, in the blue jacket, call an ambulance!" and the man in the blue jacket froze, then dialled. A woman knelt beside the collapsed man. An ambulance came within minutes. I do not know what happened to him afterwards. But I know how close I came to walking on. — Noor

qa.q: About how many people were walking past the man who collapsed?
qa.a: About thirty people were walking past.

qa.q: Why did Noor think it might not be serious when nobody stopped?
qa.a: Noor read the crowd's inaction as a sign it was not serious, each person taking the others' calm as proof; the twitching hand broke that belief and brought a sick feeling.

qa.q: What turning point led Noor to act?
qa.a: Noor saw the man's hand twitch, felt sick, and called out to one person in a blue jacket to phone an ambulance instead of waiting.

qa.q: What might the man in the blue jacket have been feeling when Noor called out?
qa.a: The man in the blue jacket probably felt startled and suddenly responsible; being named pulled him out of the crowd's passive waiting, and he dialled.

grounding: A commuter sees someone collapse while the crowd keeps walking, each reading the others' inaction as proof it is not serious.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Simran, listen, it's Jasleen, and I need to say what I saw. Last night on the market road a man kept following a woman and shouting things at her, and there were maybe twenty people around: the tea stall, two rickshaw drivers, some couples. Everyone kept walking, and so did I. All those calm faces made me think it was not serious. She was gripping her bag and walking faster. I turned around after twenty steps, walked up to the tea vendor and said loudly, "Please call the police helpline." Then the two rickshaw drivers stood near her. The man slunk off. I am shaking even now.

qa.q: How many people were around when the man followed the woman?
qa.a: There were maybe twenty people around.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen keep walking even though the woman was gripping her bag?
qa.a: Jasleen took the calm faces of the crowd as proof it was not serious, an assumption shared by everyone; afterwards the shaking shows how uneasy that decision felt.

qa.q: What choice made Jasleen turn around after twenty steps, and what did that action achieve?
qa.a: Jasleen turned back, spoke loudly to the tea vendor to call the police helpline, and this drew the rickshaw drivers to stand near the woman until the man left.

qa.q: What might the woman have been feeling while everyone walked past?
qa.a: The woman was probably frightened and alone, gripping her bag and walking faster while the crowd's silence gave her no sign anyone would help.

grounding: A commuter sees a woman harassed while the crowd keeps walking, and pluralistic ignorance makes each person read others' inaction as proof it is not serious.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: First-aid practice, community centre, Saturday. During the mock emergency twelve adults stood in a circle around the training dummy, each waiting for someone else to move. Hrithik pointed at one person after another: "You in the red shirt, phone for the ambulance. You, fetch water. You, hold the door open." Within seconds the circle turned into a team. Afterwards Latha, who had been in the red shirt, said she had felt relief at being told exactly what to do. I told the class this is why we point at one person and name a task. — Simran, trainer

qa.q: What did Hrithik tell the person in the red shirt to do?
qa.a: Hrithik told the person in the red shirt to phone for the ambulance.

qa.q: What did Latha feel when Hrithik pointed at her in the red shirt?
qa.a: Latha felt relief at being told exactly what to do; being named ended the waiting and freed her to act.

qa.q: What was the turning point that changed the circle of adults into a team?
qa.a: Hrithik pointed at one person after another and gave each a specific task, which broke the diffusion of responsibility and got action moving.

qa.q: What might it have been like for another adult in the circle who was not yet pointed at?
qa.a: That adult may have felt unsure and waiting, half hoping to be told what to do, as the circle stood before Hrithik began naming people.

grounding: An adult in an emergency points at one person and names a task, which breaks the diffusion of responsibility and gets action moving.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Tuesday, 9 pm. Today outside the pharmacy an old man fainted. A circle of people gathered, all waiting, two of them filming. I heard someone say, "Somebody call." I used my loudest voice: "You, in the green scarf, call an ambulance. You, sir, fetch the pharmacist. You, beta, bring water and a chair." Aparna, the girl in the green scarf, dialled with shaking fingers. The pharmacist came running. The man opened his eyes before the ambulance arrived. My hands are still trembling. I have never given orders in my life. — Vinita

qa.q: What did Vinita tell the girl in the green scarf to do?
qa.a: Vinita told the girl in the green scarf to call an ambulance.

qa.q: Why are Vinita's hands still trembling at night?
qa.a: Vinita is shaken and a little astonished at having taken charge; giving orders is new, and the stress of the emergency is still in the body.

qa.q: What choice by Vinita changed the situation outside the pharmacy?
qa.a: Vinita stopped waiting and pointed at specific people with specific jobs, which turned a group that waited into a group that acted.

qa.q: What might Aparna have been feeling when dialling with shaking fingers?
qa.a: Aparna probably felt nervous and suddenly responsible, but being named gave a clear task, so the fear did not stop the call.

grounding: An adult in an emergency names one person for each task, breaking diffusion of responsibility and getting action moving.

passage: I am Yamini, and I did almost nothing for our class poster on rivers. There were five of us, and I worked out that Avni always does the neat lettering and Tanvi loves drawing. So I stayed home from the group meeting and later said I had a stomach ache. On presentation day the teacher said, "Well done, group four," and I stood at the front with the others, smiling. Avni looked tired. Nobody had counted my share, so nobody noticed. I felt a bit clever and a bit small at the same time. Avni's crayon-stained fingers were the last thing I saw before the bell.

qa.q: How many children were in the group that made the river poster?
qa.a: There were five of them in the group.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Yamini have at the front of the class?
qa.a: Yamini felt a little clever for getting credit without effort and a little small, guilty about Avni looking tired; nobody counted the share so the guilt stayed private.

qa.q: What could Yamini do before the next group project so that effort is not hidden?
qa.a: Yamini could ask for a named part such as the river map, and do it, so that a share of the work is visible and the group's credit is earned.

qa.q: What might Avni be feeling with crayon-stained fingers after doing most of the lettering?
qa.a: Avni may feel tired and perhaps a little unappreciated, doing most of the work while the credit was shared out equally.

grounding: A child lets others do most of the poster because their own effort will not be noticed, and shared credit makes doing less feel safe.

passage: Note, Class 6 science charts. Group C's chart on the water cycle is neat, but during work time Kishore sat sharpening one pencil for a long stretch while three others cut, pasted and labelled. When I asked, Kishore said, "They are doing it fine, and the chart gets one mark for all of us anyway." The other three did not object; one glared. I told the group I would now note each child's part on a tick sheet and asked Kishore to take the labels. By the end of the period Kishore had written eleven labels and looked pleased. — Vijay Sir

qa.q: How many labels had Kishore written by the end of the period?
qa.a: Kishore had written eleven labels by the end of the period.

qa.q: Why did Kishore say "the chart gets one mark for all of us anyway"?
qa.a: Kishore believed that shared credit made doing less safe, and felt that effort would go unnoticed; the pencil-sharpening shows avoidance rather than refusal.

qa.q: What did Vijay Sir change that made effort visible?
qa.a: Vijay Sir noted each child's part on a tick sheet and gave Kishore a named task, labels, so individual effort could be seen without punishment.

qa.q: What might the three children who did the cutting and pasting have been feeling?
qa.a: They probably felt frustrated and unfairly burdened; the glare from one suggests resentment even though none objected aloud.

grounding: A child lets others do most of the project because shared credit makes doing less feel safe, and visible individual roles change this.

passage: In Class 4 at the community school, Ms Swati handed out four coloured cards for the group volcano model: Measurer, Painter, Builder, Reporter. "Each card has a name on the back. On Friday the Reporter tells us who did what." Sabina looked at her Painter card. Usually she let others do the work. Now her name was on the paint, and Ravi, the Reporter, would say so out loud. She mixed red and orange with care. Nobody had to nag. On Friday Ravi said, "Sabina painted the lava." Sabina's cheeks went pink, and she grinned.

qa.q: What did Ravi say about Sabina on Friday?
qa.a: Ravi said, "Sabina painted the lava."

qa.q: How did Sabina feel when hearing Ravi say it on Friday?
qa.a: Sabina felt proud and a little shy, cheeks going pink and grinning; being named made her effort count.

qa.q: What did Ms Swati do that changed how Sabina worked?
qa.a: Ms Swati gave each child a named card and a Reporter to say who did what, so effort became visible without any punishment.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ravi to be the Reporter on Friday?
qa.a: Ravi may have felt important and a bit responsible, holding the job of being fair about who did what in front of the class.

grounding: A teacher assigns each member a named part and a reporter shows who did what, so visible accountability reduces loafing without punishment.

passage: During our garden project Ganga wrote each of our names on a strip of paper with a job, watering, weeding, seed labels, sketching, and stuck the strips on the board. Arohi, who usually disappeared when there was work, read her strip: "seed labels." She grumbled but sat down and wrote nine labels. When the teacher came round, Ganga pointed at the board and said, "You can see who did what." Nobody argued. I could not tell whether Arohi liked her job, but she stayed until the last label was done.

qa.q: How many seed labels did Arohi write?
qa.a: Arohi wrote nine labels.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when sticking the named strips on the board?
qa.a: Ganga was probably hopeful and a little determined that the work would be shared fairly, which shows when Ganga points at the board and says the teacher can see who did what.

qa.q: What choice by Ganga made it hard for anyone to coast?
qa.a: Ganga gave every child a named job on the board, so who did what was visible without anyone being told off.

qa.q: What was it like for Arohi to find her own name next to "seed labels"?
qa.a: Arohi probably felt annoyed and a bit cornered, since she grumbled, yet with her name on the job she sat down and wrote all nine labels.

grounding: A child assigns each member a named part and shows who did what, so visible accountability shrinks loafing without punishment.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 9 group assignment. During the poster work Bhavna spent most of the period "finding a marker" while the other three researched and wrote. Bhavna told me later, "They will finish it, they always do." Bhavna did not look proud, and looked away when I said the other three seemed worn out. The three said nothing, though one rolled her eyes and another sighed. I spoke with Bhavna privately and asked which part felt doable, and Bhavna picked the summary. I will check in on Friday. — Jahnavi Ma'am

qa.q: Which part did Bhavna pick after the private talk?
qa.a: Bhavna picked the summary.

qa.q: What does Bhavna's looking away when the others are called worn out suggest about how Bhavna feels?
qa.a: It suggests guilt and unease; Bhavna assumed the diligent ones would finish, and seems to sense it is not fair.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi Ma'am do that could change Bhavna's contribution?
qa.a: Jahnavi Ma'am spoke with Bhavna privately, asked which part felt doable and planned to check in on Friday, which gives a clear task and follow-up.

qa.q: What might the child who rolled her eyes be feeling?
qa.a: She may feel irritated and taken for granted, doing more than her share while saying nothing aloud.

grounding: A teenager does the minimum in a group project, assuming the diligent ones will finish, feeling a little guilty but rarely admitting it.

passage: Sunday. The group assignment on renewable energy is due Wednesday. Chetan messaged, "Harish, which section are you taking?" I sent a thumbs-up and did nothing. I wrote "will do tonight" three times. Priyal and Chetan are the serious ones. They will finish it; they always do. I feel a bit clever for sleeping in and a bit rotten, as if I am cheating without doing anything I could be blamed for. Nobody will know my slides are missing until the last minute. Last time Chetan just added them. I hate that I am counting on that. Maybe tomorrow I will actually do one slide. — Harish

qa.q: What did Harish send in reply to Chetan's message?
qa.a: Harish sent a thumbs-up and did nothing.

qa.q: Why does Harish feel both clever and rotten?
qa.a: Harish feels clever for getting away with doing nothing and rotten for relying on others; the guilt is private but real.

qa.q: What small step could Harish take today to break the pattern?
qa.a: Harish could tell Chetan which section will be done and by when, then finish one slide tonight, so the promise is visible.

qa.q: What might Chetan be feeling after adding Harish's slides last time?
qa.a: Chetan may feel tired and quietly resentful, having covered for Harish without saying so, and worried about being the one to fix it again.

grounding: A teenager does the minimum in a group project, assuming the diligent ones will finish, feeling a little guilty but clever, and rarely admits it.

passage: In the small-town school, Class 10, Manjula's group of four had to finish a file on soil types for Monday. The other three had promised sections. By Sunday afternoon Manjula had written all of them, redrawn two maps and stapled the pages. Pradeep, the group leader, had sent only a text: "you are so good at this, thanks!" Manjula wanted to say it was not fair, but she thought of being called bossy, like last time, and typed, "Fine, no problem." She pressed the staples down so hard the paper tore. Then she put the torn corner in her bag and told nobody.

qa.q: What did Pradeep send to Manjula on Sunday?
qa.a: Pradeep sent a text: "you are so good at this, thanks!"

qa.q: Why did Manjula type "Fine, no problem" although she wanted to say it was not fair?
qa.a: Manjula feared being called bossy, so the anger stayed hidden and built quietly; the torn paper shows the strength of that unspoken resentment.

qa.q: What could Manjula say to the group before the next deadline?
qa.a: Manjula could name the sections she finished and ask each person to send theirs by a set time, framed as sharing the work rather than blaming anyone.

qa.q: What might Pradeep be thinking when sending only a text of thanks?
qa.a: Pradeep may believe the praise is enough, or not realise how heavy the work was; the cheerful text suggests not seeing Manjula's resentment.

grounding: A conscientious student ends up doing most of a shared task and grows resentful, fearing that complaining will look bossy.

passage: In a Vancouver Grade 10 class, Kwame stayed until six on Thursday finishing the group science presentation. Xin had promised the graphs and Ines the conclusion; both arrived on Friday with nothing but jokes. Kwame's jaw tightened. "We can share the rest at lunch?" Ines suggested brightly. "Sure," said Kwame. Inside, Kwame was seething. During the presentation Xin got the biggest smile from the teacher. Kwame said nothing then either, only smiled thinly, and wrote in a private notebook, "Next time I will say it early. But saying it feels bossy."

qa.q: Until what time did Kwame stay on Thursday?
qa.a: Kwame stayed until six on Thursday finishing the group science presentation.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling when saying "Sure" to Ines?
qa.a: Kwame was seething with anger inside while sounding polite; the tight jaw shows resentment being swallowed to avoid looking bossy.

qa.q: What could Kwame do at the start of the next group project?
qa.a: Kwame could suggest early who does what and when, and check in midweek, so the imbalance is visible before it becomes resentment.

qa.q: How might Ines have seen Friday's lunch offer?
qa.a: Ines probably saw it as a friendly solution and may not have noticed how much work Kwame had done; the bright tone suggests no awareness of the anger.

grounding: A conscientious student ends up doing most of a shared task and grows resentful, fearing that complaining will look bossy.

passage: Dear Preeti, I have to write it down. Our project team has five people, and one of them, Vivek, has done almost nothing for three weeks. Vivek is also my friend, the one who covered for me when Mum was ill. So when Jyoti asked in the meeting, "Has everyone finished their part?" I looked at my notes and said nothing. So did Dev and Sara. We all know. Jyoti is now doing double, and yesterday Jyoti stopped smiling at us. The trust in the team feels thinner every day. I am writing to ask you: how do I speak to Vivek without ending the friendship? — Sunaina

qa.q: How long has Vivek done almost nothing for the project?
qa.a: Vivek has done almost nothing for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina look at the notes and say nothing when Jyoti asked?
qa.a: Sunaina wanted to protect the friendship with Vivek, who once covered for Sunaina; the silence came from loyalty mixed with guilt.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do before writing off the friendship or the team?
qa.a: Sunaina could talk to Vivek privately and kindly, ask what is going on, and then raise the shared workload openly with the team.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel doing double and no longer smiling at the others?
qa.a: Jyoti probably feels overloaded and let down, and the loss of smiles suggests the unfairness is starting to turn into resentment.

grounding: Team members see one member not pulling their weight and stay silent to protect the relationship, and the unfairness slowly damages trust.

passage: Payal, can I tell you something I am not proud of? I am Jeevan, remember, the one who said everything was "fine". In our final-year team Arjun did hardly any of the lab reports. Everybody knew. But Arjun is the guy who brought all of us tiffin when we were stuck in the lab till midnight, so nobody wanted to be the one to say it. Meena did Arjun's share twice. I saw her face fall each time and said nothing. Six weeks in, the four of us barely spoke at lunch, and the tension was so thick you could cut it. It was not fine, and I knew.

qa.q: How many times did Meena do Arjun's share?
qa.a: Meena did Arjun's share twice.

qa.q: Why did nobody want to say anything about Arjun's missing work?
qa.a: They liked Arjun for bringing tiffin during late nights and feared spoiling the friendship; loyalty and awkwardness kept the group silent.

qa.q: What could Jeevan have done the first time Meena's face fell?
qa.a: Jeevan could have checked with Meena privately, then raised the imbalance kindly with Arjun, before the silence grew into tension.

qa.q: What might Meena have been feeling when doing Arjun's share and no one spoke up?
qa.a: Meena probably felt tired, unappreciated and a bit invisible; the fallen face shows hurt at the silence of the others.

grounding: Team members see one member not pulling their weight and stay silent to protect the relationship, and the unfairness slowly damages the team's trust.

subtype: Feeling anonymous in a large team [Actor]
passage: Wednesday. Our hackathon team has thirty-two people and I have been doing very little. Nobody knows who wrote what in the shared file, and everything goes under "Team 7". I skipped the last two calls and nobody messaged. Sabina, the coordinator, said "great work, everyone" and I felt nothing. It made me think of last term, when I did the whole marine-life slide for a small group. Everyone praised that one, and I stayed up till two. So maybe it is not laziness, more that this feels like shouting into a big hall. Tomorrow I will ask Sabina whether I can take one named part. — Rehana

qa.q: How many people are on the hackathon team?
qa.a: The hackathon team has thirty-two people.

qa.q: Why does Rehana feel nothing when Sabina says "great work, everyone"?
qa.a: Rehana feels anonymous and unseen, as if the effort cannot be traced or would not matter; the praise is for everyone, so it does not reach anyone.

qa.q: What choice does Rehana make at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Rehana decides to ask Sabina for one named part, so the work is visible, as it was when Rehana did the marine-life slide.

qa.q: What might Sabina, as coordinator of thirty-two people, be seeing about Rehana's calls?
qa.a: Sabina may not have noticed the skipped calls among so many people, which shows how easily one person's absence goes unseen in a big team.

grounding: A student in a big group feels their contribution cannot be traced, so effort drops, though the same student works hard when their part is visible.

passage: In the polytechnic in a small town the group had a robot project due in ten days. Shalini had not turned up for the last three sessions or sent her drawings. Jatin caught Shalini at the bicycle stand after class, away from the others. "You seem off lately. Is something wrong, or is the work confusing?" Shalini looked down for a moment. "My father is in hospital in the city, and I go back on weekends. I did not want to say." Jatin nodded. "Then tell me which part is hard right now, and we will split the rest." Shalini breathed out. At the next meeting Ravi asked loudly why Shalini was missing, and Jatin said, "It is sorted."

qa.q: Where did Jatin speak to Shalini?
qa.a: Jatin caught Shalini at the bicycle stand after class, away from the others.

qa.q: What might Shalini have been feeling before telling Jatin about the hospital?
qa.a: Shalini was probably worried and tense, carrying a private worry about a family member and not wanting to say; the breath out shows relief when Jatin listened.

qa.q: What made Jatin's private question more helpful than raising it in the meeting?
qa.a: Jatin asked away from the others, without accusing, and offered to split the work, which let Shalini explain and kept the team from judging without knowing.

qa.q: Why might Ravi have asked loudly why Shalini was missing?
qa.a: Ravi may be annoyed at the extra work and unaware of the reason; without the private talk, absence looks like plain avoidance.

grounding: A team member asks a coasting member what is going on in private before escalating, and there is a hidden reason such as family illness.

passage: In a Manchester study group Mei had not touched the shared slides for two weeks. Kai and Priya were quietly furious. Dalia caught Mei at the vending machine. "Hey, no pressure, but what is going on? I noticed your part is empty." Mei shrugged and looked at the machine. "Honestly? I just have not felt like doing it. It seemed boring, and you all were doing fine." Dalia waited a moment. "Okay. It matters to me that the work is shared, so can you take the last slide by Thursday?" Mei sighed. "Fine." Dalia did not add a lecture. By Friday the slide was there, with a note: "Sorry, it was avoidance."

qa.q: How long had Mei not touched the shared slides?
qa.a: Mei had not touched the shared slides for two weeks.

qa.q: Why did Mei say "It seemed boring, and you all were doing fine"?
qa.a: Mei was avoiding the work and assuming others would cover it; the shrug shows little guilt at first, though the note later shows some.

qa.q: What did Dalia do that got the slide done without a fight?
qa.a: Dalia asked privately and calmly, said sharing mattered, and asked for one clear slide by Thursday without a lecture.

qa.q: What might Kai and Priya be feeling while Mei's part stays empty?
qa.a: Kai and Priya are probably angry and worried about the deadline, but quiet about it, letting resentment build without anyone speaking.

grounding: A team member asks a coasting member what is going on in private before escalating, and the reason turns out to be plain avoidance.
